doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Nat King Cole as a justified success
summary: Asked who deserves his record sales, Mancuso picks Nat King Cole, discussing his diction, Hollywood neighbourhood story and foreign-language records.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: In your book you have a lot of detailed charts about record sales and so forth. In your mind, can you pick out an artist that you think whose record sales are justified, whose talent is justified by record sales. Who is an artist that comes to mind?
You know Alabama, went out there, even whitened his face, oh it was terrible.

No. At one point before he got to California, it was so hard for a black man in the deep south, as you can imagine, he had to whiten up, he thought. Oh it’s scary. There’s a documentary that shows when he was doing it. But when he went out there, and you know, Central Avenue, and all he did with those early records was just play jazz. Cab Calloway claims that he tried to convince Nat that he had a little stutter and he was embarrassed to sing because he couldn’t really. He says, “You stand in front of a mirror and you pronounce the words slowly. And you will be able to improve your diction.” I © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-
don’t know if that’s all he did, but I’ll tell you he was one of the most articulated singers in the history of American pop music.
You know just on the way here today, I don’t know if it was the Buffalo station or Toronto, they played him singing “Stardust.” Good Lord.
So I’m glad you picked him.

You know, and what I didn’t realize, that he wanted to live in Hollywood. Because he was out there, Capitol Records, you know, the house that Nat built. And he had moved into this neighborhood, and it was all whites. And so the people came to him and they said, “Listen,” you know, “we’ve got some problems here.” You know, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah. They didn’t come out and say that he was the problem, but he knew what they were talking about. And Nat said, “Well you know, my wife and I meant to talk to you people about this.” You know, he goes, “Some of the people are leaving their garbage out and this is a really ritzy neighborhood, and so I hope we’re going to put some of that garbage away because we like it here and we’re not moving.”
He headed them off at the pass.

He made these records of his hits in Japanese, in Spanish, in French, in Italian. He couldn’t speak them. But he must have worked so hard on his diction that he could learn the words — not read the stuff — he learned the words and then he would take trips to all these places. That’s how rich he got. We didn’t know anything about it. I didn’t know anything about it. It was unbelievable. What a remarkable guy.
